The [Bitwise Calculator](/bitwise-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts on integers — in decimal, binary and hex. Enter your first number (A), second number (B) and operation and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Bitwise operations work on the individual bits of integers — the ones and zeros a computer actually stores. AND keeps a bit only where both numbers have it, OR keeps it where either has it, XOR keeps it where exactly one has it, and NOT flips every bit. Shifts move bits left (multiplying by powers of two) or right (dividing). They are the building blocks of flags, permissions, compression, graphics and cryptography. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Bitwise Calculator

Start by entering your first number (A), then entering your second number (B) and finally choosing your operation from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the first number (A) — whole numbers only.
2. Enter the second number (B), unless you chose NOT, which uses A alone.
3. Choose the operation and read the result in decimal, binary and hexadecimal.

## Formula

AND: 1 & 1 = 1, otherwise 0. OR: 0 | 0 = 0, otherwise 1. XOR: 1 ^ 0 = 1, 1 ^ 1 = 0. Left shift A << n = A × 2ⁿ. Right shift A >> n = floor(A ÷ 2ⁿ).

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Bitwise Calculator](/bitwise-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. 12 is 1100 in binary and 10 is 1010. 12 AND 10 = 8 (1000), 12 OR 10 = 14 (1110), 12 XOR 10 = 6 (0110), and 12 << 1 = 24. Try the same figures in the [Bitwise Calculator](/bitwise-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (First number (A): 12, Second number (B): 10, Operation: AND (A & B)), the [Bitwise Calculator](/bitwise-calculator) returns Result (AND): 8, Binary: 1000, Hexadecimal: 0x8, A in binary: 1100, B in binary: 1010. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## What bitwise operations are for

A single integer can hold many yes/no flags: each bit is one flag, so checking a permission is one AND operation instead of a whole list of booleans. Graphics code packs red, green, blue and alpha into one 32-bit number and pulls the channels out with shifts and masks. Compression, checksums and hash functions are all built from AND, OR, XOR and shifts — fast operations that map directly onto what the processor does.

## Shifts are fast multiplication and division

Shifting left by n multiplies by 2ⁿ, and shifting right divides by 2ⁿ (rounding down for positive numbers): 12 << 1 = 24, 12 >> 1 = 6. Compilers use this trick whenever they can, which is why powers of two appear so often in computing — buffer sizes, image dimensions and memory pages are usually powers of two.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- XOR with the same value twice returns the original — the basis of simple encryption and swap tricks.
- Use AND with a mask (e.g. x & 1) to test a single bit, such as whether a number is odd.
- JavaScript bitwise operations work on 32-bit integers — numbers beyond that range wrap.

## Frequently asked questions

### What does bitwise AND do?

It compares each bit of two numbers and keeps a 1 only where both numbers have a 1. 12 (1100) AND 10 (1010) = 8 (1000). Try it with your own numbers in the [Bitwise Calculator](/bitwise-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is XOR used for?

XOR keeps a bit where the two inputs differ. It toggles flags, detects differences, and is the core of many checksums and simple ciphers — XORing twice with the same key returns the original value. Try it with your own numbers in the [Bitwise Calculator](/bitwise-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why do shifts multiply and divide by two?

Moving all bits one place left doubles the value, just as adding a zero to a decimal number multiplies it by ten. Each place left is another factor of two. Try it with your own numbers in the [Bitwise Calculator](/bitwise-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
